idiom_name: empty marker type recognised by compile-time constraint or run-time type test
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare a type with no members whose only purpose is to be implemented, have marked types declare conformance, and let consumers recognise the mark - through a compile-time constraint on the marked type set or through a run-time type test. Keep the marker empty and document its consumer; the mark is inherited by all subtypes, so only mark types whose claim holds for the whole hierarchy. Where the language offers metadata constructs, the choice is Effective Java Item 41: use a marker type when substitutability or compile-time constraints matter, an annotation when the signal is descriptive.
pitfalls: Marking every type 'just in case' turns the marker into a default supertype that no consumer ever reads.
A mark whose claim the compiler cannot check (serializable, thread-safe) can be a lie; only mark what holds for every instance and subtype.
Hybrid markers that also declare methods blur the boundary between metadata and behavioural contract.

Wrong move: mark a broad superclass for a capability that one subtype cannot honour -> inherited conformance makes the claim apply to that subtype and forces runtime exceptions or lies -> instead mark the narrowest types whose entire hierarchy satisfies the property.

Wrong move: declare Send, Sync or Sendable because a type currently passes tests -> unchecked conformance can let unsynchronised state cross a concurrency boundary -> instead derive the marker from safe fields and invariants, or isolate unchecked implementations behind synchronization.

Wrong move: replace a behavioural interface with an empty marker and reflective method lookup -> callers lose a compile-time contract and fail only when the method is absent -> instead keep the behavioural interface and use a separate marker only for orthogonal metadata.
